j: If your spouse was legally married to someone else when you got married and that person is still living, you can seek an annulment. This ground can be asserted at any time during the lifetime of the parties. This marriage is void under the law. DOM § 6

If one of the parties to the marriage was underage at the time of the marriage you can seek an annulment. This ground can be asserted until the underage party is legal of the age of consent. This is a voidable ground for marriage. See Part I Marriage section above. DOM § 7, DOM § 140

If one the parties is physical incapable of sexual relations with the other spouse at the time of the marriage, and this is not known to the other spouse at the time of the marriage, the court may grant an annulment within five years of the marriage. This is a voidable ground. DOM § 7, DOM § 140

attribution: Mathematics Methods for Early Childhood by Janet Stramel, CC BY 4.0

sections.t: The Importance of Early Childhood Mathematics
j: Mathematicians often work for an extended time on a single problem. Allow your students ample time to work on a problem.
Mathematicians collaborate with their colleagues and study the work of others. Allow your students to collaborate, argue, consult, defend, ask, explain, and pose questions to others.

Mathematicians must prove for themselves that their solution is correct. Children must also prove to themselves that they have the correct solution. Give students time to think and discuss. Don’t be too quick to tell a student their answer is correct or incorrect; instead ask the student to explain their answer.

The problems mathematicians work on are complex. Good problems ask students to find innovative solutions without a time limit. Problems should spark children’s thinking, rather than promote rote memorization.

Mathematicians get satisfaction from the problem-solving process and take pride in their solutions. Children will understand the concepts and procedures more if they are allowed to use their own thinking processes. This also allows children to make connections to prior knowledge and real-life experiences.
Mathematicians use unsuccessful attempts as stepping-stones to solutions. We need to emphasize mathematical thinking rather than just getting the correct answer.

Durkheim’s consensus view of crime suggests that it is society that determines what is criminal and that crime is normal as it establishes moral boundaries of a community.

For Merton, anomie is a condition whereby society exerts pressure on the individual to achieve culturally defined goals but does not provide the institutional means to achieve them. Merton’s macro-level theory was called strain theory.
The Chicago School had a distinctly macro-level ecological approach to studying crime that involved concentric zones in cities, with certain zones marked by greater degrees of disorganisation.
Cohen’s subcultural theory of delinquency views juvenile delinquency as a particular type of subculture, and offers an explanation for crimes committed by juveniles that do not have a rational goal.

j: The dominant positivistic paradigm of criminology focused on identifying and studying causes of crime that could then be corrected, while most critical criminology adopts a critical social science position that is anti-positivist.
Critical criminology encompasses a set of concepts and ideas examining how crime and criminal justice agencies are used as a form of social power that benefits some groups over others.
The work of Karl Marx forms the foundation of critical criminology; he argues that criminal law in its origin emerged as a tool of control for elites.

For Marx, power is always connected to economic power and how it manifests at the level of the state, while Foucault’s work broadens the analysis of power and looks to the emergence of discourses and how these are translated into techniques or methods of power.

Garland builds on Foucault’s work and examines how the system moved from a system of punishment and rehabilitative justice to one of safety and risk management. He refers to this as a new culture of crime control.
Contemporary critical criminology focuses on police and penal abolition.
Convict criminology is an approach to criminology that privileges the voices and standpoints of persons who have been criminalised or who have been affected by the criminal justice system.
Many methods of critical criminology are anti-positivist in orientation. These methods include historical ethnography, qualitative methods, institutional ethnography and critical discourse analyses.

Cultural criminology is a critical perspective that examines social and economic shifts in the era of late modernity.
Cultural criminology tries to bring the experience of crime to life by focusing on the foreground, rather than abstract background factors, like age and social class.

Cultural criminology borrows from several sociological theories of deviance, including the Chicago School of Sociology, the new deviance theory (which included subcultural theory and labelling theory), Matza and Syke’s techniques of neutralization, and Young and Cohen’s moral panic theory.

The four key features of cultural criminology are: the concept that culture is foundational and is about collective meaning and identity; the concept that culture is dynamic; the idea that we are living in an era known as late modernity; and the commitment to critical and politically engaged research.
Cultural criminology shifts the analysis of criminology to the immediate feelings and experiences of the criminal event itself, such as excitement.
Boredom and pleasure are key concepts that cultural criminology uses to make sense of actions that appear senseless.
Methods used by cultural criminologists include instant ethnography; other sensory data and approaches are also used in their work.
Media and pop culture are important sites for cultural criminology to analyse the collision of culture, crime and control.

Cultural criminologists employ the concept of loops and spirals to encapsulate the complex and non-linear way meaning flows through media and popular culture and the dynamic interplay between crime, control and media representation.

While cultural criminology could be a valuable approach to analysing the way art and culture are used to both further the project of colonialism and to promote social change, cultural criminological analysis of colonialism and anti-colonial protest has yet to be written.

sections.t: 15.2 Crimes of the Powerful are White-Collar Crimes

j: White-collar crime is defined by Sutherland as a crime committed by a person of respectability and high social status in the course of their occupation.

Occupational crime includes thefts against businesses that involve employees, executives, or owners, for personal benefit, while corporate crime is when an individual uses their position within an organisation to illegally benefit corporate interests.
Corporate crime includes corporate theft, corporate tax evasion, and corporate violence.
Many white-collar crimes are financial crimes including banking frauds, price-fixing, illegal monopolies, and insider trading.
Political crime refers to governmental or political party officials engaging in illegal and improper activity for personal gain. Political crime includes influence peddling.

State-organised crime is defined as acts defined by law as criminal and committed by state officials in pursuit of their job as representatives of the state. These include illegal surveillance, c oup d’états, assassinations, and illegal wars.
Colonialism constitutes the largest program of state-organised harms in world history.

Crimes of the powerful pose unique challenges for the criminal justice system, victims, marginalised groups, academics, and other stakeholders. Central amongst these challenges relates to the role of the powerful in determining what is defined as a crime in the first place.

Social network analysis is useful because it encourages us to look at relationships, exchanges, conflicts, and opportunities rather than assuming that gang boundaries are obvious or permanent.

Contemporary gang involvement among some Indigenous people must be understood in relation to the structural harms of colonialism.
British Columbia provides an important case study because many contemporary gang conflicts do not fit older images of territorially fixed, ethnically uniform gangs.

j: Environmental criminology is a branch of criminology focused on the criminal event and not the individual criminal.
Theories under this approach examine the spatial distribution of crime, victimisation, or offenders in society.

Green criminology represents the branch of criminology that deals with research into criminality against the environment and associated phenomena, while environmental criminology is a branch of criminology that deals with researching physical and social determinations of patterns of criminal behaviour.
Environmental criminology is closely connected with situational crime prevention.
The four key environmental theories of crime include: routine activity theory, geometric theory, rational choice theory, and pattern theory.
Much of the contemporary environmental criminological research has focused on where offenders tend to commit crimes.

By emphasizing the relationship between place, opportunity, and routine human behaviour, environmental criminology allows researchers and policymakers to move beyond individual motivations and consider how the built environment and social structures shape crime patterns.
Environmental criminology theories can both help shed light on as well as hinder our understanding of the lived experiences of Indigenous peoples.

j: Restorative justice is a theory of justice and is part of the critical tradition in criminology.

Restorative justice aims to repair relationships harmed by crime and is related to transformative justice, which highlights the essential need to change social structures that perpetuate injustice and inequality.
Restorative justice aims to put victims’ needs at the centre of the justice process and to encourage greater community engagement through inclusive and collaborative processes.
Different definitions of restorative justice often have a different emphasis on either encounter, reparative, or transformative dimensions.
Restorative justice aims to meaningfully include three stakeholders in the justice process: victim, offender, and community.
Key principles of restorative justice practices include offender accountability and voluntary victim/survivor participation and choice. Community members might also be included.
Restorative justice models include victim-offender dialogue, conferencing, and circles.
While restorative justice and Indigenous practices are similar, these terms are not interchangeable.
Restorative justice has many benefits for victims/survivors, the offender and the community.

Measure or bar —Beats are grouped into measures or bars. The first beat is usually the strongest, and in most music, most of the bars have the same number of beats. This sets up an underlying pattern in the pulse of the music: for example, strong-weak-strong-weak-strong-weak, or strong-weak-weak-strong-weak-weak.
